notes: Redraft addresses three fact-check findings from the prior draft: (1) "Six Woes" now cites all six woe-oracles including the previously-missing 29:15 ("Woe unto them that seek deep to hide their counsel from the LORD"), restoring the count named in the tier; (2) Hezekiah's genealogy note now uses the KJV's own spelling "Hizkiah" for the ancestor named in Zephaniah 1:1 and explicitly does not assert this is the same man as King Hezekiah, since the text itself never makes that identification; (3) two previously-uncovered, heavily-recognized standalone passages — 9:6-7 ("Unto us a child is born") and 40:1-11 ("Comfort ye, comfort ye my people") — now each have their own law-tier. All genealogical claims are scoped strictly to what Isaiah's own text states (e.g. Ahaz son of Jotham son of Uzziah is drawn only from 7:1, not imported from Kings/Chronicles). Flagged naming notes: Amoz (Isaiah's father, 1:1) vs. Amos (separate minor prophet) — different names, easily confused in English; Hizkiah (Zephaniah 1:1, outside this book) vs. Hezekiah — a real KJV spelling difference, relationship unstated.

characters.name: Isaiah

genealogy.note: Isaiah's father Amoz (spelled with 'z', Isaiah 1:1) is distinct from the minor prophet Amos (spelled with 's') — a common English-spelling confusion between two unrelated names/figures. Isaiah's wife is called only 'the prophetess' (8:3) and never given a personal name.

funFacts: Ministered across the reigns of four kings of Judah — Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (1:1).
His prophetic call vision (ch. 6) came 'in the year that king Uzziah died' and included a seraph touching his lips with a live coal from the altar (6:6-7).
Walked naked and barefoot for three years as a prophetic sign against Egypt and Ethiopia (20:2-3).
Both of his sons carry prophetic sign-names: Shearjashub ('a remnant shall return') and Mahershalalhashbaz ('hasten to the spoil, hurry to the prey').

verses.note: Superscription naming Isaiah son of Amoz and the four kings of Judah under whom he prophesied.
Call vision in the temple; a seraph purges his lips with a live coal; he answers 'Here am I; send me.'
Sent by the LORD to meet Ahaz at the conduit of the upper pool, taking his son Shearjashub.
Instructed to write and then name his newborn son Mahershalalhashbaz.
Commanded to walk naked and barefoot three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia.
Delivers the LORD's answering oracles to Hezekiah during the Assyrian crisis.
Comes to the dying Hezekiah with a message from the LORD.
Confronts Hezekiah after the Babylonian envoys' visit, foretelling exile to Babylon.

characters.name: Ahaz

genealogy.note: Isaiah 7:1 states the line explicitly: 'Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah' — three generations named in one verse, entirely within this book.

funFacts: Faced with an invasion by Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel, his and the people's 'heart was moved as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind' (7:2).
Refused Isaiah's invitation to ask the LORD for any sign, 'either in the depth, or in the height above' (7:11-12).
The Immanuel sign (7:14) was given to the 'house of David' despite, not because of, his refusal.

verses.note: Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, march on Jerusalem but cannot prevail; Ahaz's court is shaken.
Isaiah meets Ahaz and tells him the two invading kings are mere 'smoking firebrands,' soon to fail.
Ahaz refuses to ask for a confirming sign from the LORD.
Isaiah rebukes him ('is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also?') and gives the Immanuel sign regardless.

characters.name: Hezekiah

genealogy.note: Isaiah never states Hezekiah's parentage directly within its own text (unlike Ahaz's explicit father/grandfather chain in 7:1) — 1:1 lists him last among 'Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah' in reign order, which implies but does not assert succession or parentage. Separately, Zephaniah 1:1 (outside this book) names an ancestor spelled 'Hizkiah' in the KJV — a genuine KJV spelling variant, not 'Hezekiah' — and that text never identifies him as King Hezekiah of Judah; whether they are the same man is an open, unstated question, not confirmed here.

funFacts: When Sennacherib's field commander Rabshakeh taunted Jerusalem, Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and went into the house of the LORD (37:1).
Spread Sennacherib's threatening letter before the LORD in the temple and prayed over it (37:14-15).
When told he would die of his sickness, wept, and was granted fifteen more years of life, confirmed by the shadow moving backward ten degrees on 'the sun dial of Ahaz' (38:1-8).
Left a personal psalm of thanksgiving after his recovery, recorded in full (38:9-20).
Showed all his treasures to the Babylonian envoys of Merodach-baladan, prompting Isaiah's prophecy that his house's wealth and descendants would one day be carried to Babylon (39:2-7).

verses.note: Sennacherib invades Judah 'in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah.'
Hezekiah's response to the Assyrian threat: torn clothes, sackcloth, the house of the LORD.
Prays over Sennacherib's letter in the temple.
Receives Isaiah's answering oracle of deliverance.
Illness, the promise of fifteen added years, and the sign of the sun dial of Ahaz moving backward.
Hezekiah's own written psalm of thanksgiving after recovery.
Receives Merodach-baladan's envoys, shows his treasures, and hears Isaiah's prophecy of future Babylonian exile.

characters.name: Sennacherib

genealogy.note: Isaiah names three sons only at his death: Adrammelech and Sharezer, who kill him, and Esarhaddon, who succeeds him (37:38). None of the three has any other role or entry in this index.

funFacts: King of Assyria; took 'all the defenced cities of Judah' before turning on Jerusalem itself (36:1).
Sent his field commander Rabshakeh with a great army and a taunting speech aimed at Hezekiah and the people on the wall (36:2-20).
Also sent a written letter mocking the LORD's ability to deliver Jerusalem, which Hezekiah spread out before the LORD in the temple (37:9-14).
The angel of the LORD struck 'a hundred and fourscore and five thousand' in the Assyrian camp in a single night (37:36).
Later assassinated by his own sons Adrammelech and Sharezer while worshipping in the house of his god Nisroch; his son Esarhaddon reigned in his place (37:38).

verses.note: Invades Judah's fortified cities and sends Rabshakeh with an army to Jerusalem.
Hears that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia has come out to fight him and sends Hezekiah a further threatening letter.
185,000 in his camp struck dead by the angel of the LORD in one night.
Withdraws to Nineveh and is later killed by his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer while worshipping Nisroch his god; succeeded by his son Esarhaddon.

characters.name: Cyrus

genealogy.note: No genealogy is given for Cyrus in Isaiah; he is a Persian king named only in the context of prophecy, generations before his own lifetime relative to Isaiah's ministry.

funFacts: Named directly by Isaiah roughly a century and a half before his birth, an unusually specific prophetic naming.
Called the LORD's 'shepherd' (44:28) and the LORD's 'anointed' (45:1) — the only foreign king in the book given the title 'anointed.'
Prophesied to authorize the rebuilding of Jerusalem and its temple foundation (44:28) and to 'let go my captives, not for price nor reward' (45:13).

verses.note: Named as the LORD's shepherd who will say of Jerusalem, 'Thou shalt be built,' and of the temple, 'Thy foundation shall be laid.'
Called the LORD's anointed, whose right hand the LORD has held, to subdue nations before him.
Raised up 'in righteousness' to build the LORD's city and release the captives without price or reward.

characters.name: Shearjashub
characters.perkNote: His very name — 'a remnant shall return' — is itself a standing sign of hope accompanying his father on the mission to Ahaz (7:3), reinforcing Isaiah's message.

genealogy.note: Named in 7:3 only; his name functions as a prophetic sign ('a remnant shall return').

funFacts: Only appears once, silently accompanying his father to meet Ahaz (7:3) — the text records no words of his own.

verses.note: Taken by Isaiah to meet Ahaz at the conduit of the upper pool; his name itself is the message.

characters.name: Mahershalalhashbaz
characters.perkNote: His name — 'hasten to the spoil, hurry to the prey' — is a sign-name announcing the swift, imminent plunder of Damascus and Samaria by Assyria (8:1-4), a fast-forward on judgment already decreed.

genealogy.note: Named in both 8:1 (written on a great roll before his birth) and 8:3 (spoken at his birth).

funFacts: Before he could say 'my father' or 'my mother,' the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria would be taken by the king of Assyria (8:4).

verses.note: The LORD instructs Isaiah to write the child's name on a great roll before witnesses.
Born to Isaiah and 'the prophetess'; his name is confirmed, with a timetable tied to Assyria's conquests.

characters.name: Eliakim
characters.perkNote: Given 'the key of the house of David' and made 'a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem' (22:20-22); still standing at Hezekiah's side through the whole Assyrian crisis (36:3, 22; 37:2).

genealogy.note: Called 'the son of Hilkiah' throughout (22:20, 36:3, 36:22) — a different Hilkiah than any high priest of that name in other books; Isaiah gives no further identification.

funFacts: Isaiah 22:23-24 pictures him as 'a nail in a sure place,' with his father's household hung on him 'all vessels of small quantity.'

Isaiah 22:25 later pictures 'the nail' being cut down and falling — the text does not explicitly re-name Eliakim as the one meant, so whether this extends to his own eventual fall is not stated outright.
Titled 'over the household' when he appears again during the Assyrian crisis (36:3, 22; 37:2).

verses.note: The LORD calls him 'my servant Eliakim,' clothes him with Shebna's robe, and gives him 'the key of the house of David.'
Described as a peg/nail fastened in a sure place, bearing the weight of his father's house.
Comes out to meet Rabshakeh, titled 'which was over the household,' alongside Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder.
Sent by Hezekiah, with Shebna and the elders of the priests, to Isaiah.

characters.name: Shebna
characters.perkNote: Originally 'the treasurer, which is over the house' (22:15) before being demoted; still functioning as court scribe during the Assyrian crisis (36:3, 22; 37:2).

genealogy.note: Given no patronymic, unlike Eliakim ('son of Hilkiah'); Isaiah gives him no family details at all.

funFacts: Rebuked by name for hewing himself a sepulchre on high and for his 'chariots of glory' (22:15-18) — the LORD says he will be tossed away 'like a ball into a large country' and die there.
Appears again with the reduced title 'the scribe' during Sennacherib's invasion (36:3, 22; 37:2), suggesting the demotion foretold in ch. 22 had taken effect by then.

verses.note: Rebuked as 'this treasurer, which is over the house' and told he will be removed from his station and die in a foreign land.
Appears as 'Shebna the scribe' alongside Eliakim and Joah before Rabshakeh.
Sent with Eliakim and the elders of the priests to Isaiah.

characters.name: Joah
characters.perkNote: The court recorder present at both confrontations with Rabshakeh (36:3, 22), keeping the official account alongside Eliakim and Shebna.

genealogy.note: Called 'Asaph's son' both times he appears (36:3, 36:22) — a different Asaph than the Levitical musician/psalm-writer of that name, as Isaiah gives no further identification linking them.

funFacts: Never speaks in Isaiah's account; named only by title and patronymic, 'the recorder,' alongside Eliakim and Shebna.

verses.note: Named as 'Joah, Asaph's son, the recorder,' part of the delegation that meets Rabshakeh.
Reports back to Hezekiah with torn clothes after hearing Rabshakeh's words.

characters.name: Rabshakeh
characters.perkNote: Sent by Sennacherib with a great army specifically to deliver and amplify the king's own words ('Thus saith the great king,' 36:4) — his taunting speech is presented as Sennacherib's message, not his own agenda.

genealogy.note: 'Rabshakeh' is most likely a title (a chief officer) rather than a personal name, though Isaiah's text never gives him any other name and treats it as if one.

funFacts: Delivers his speech in Hebrew, deliberately audible to the people on the wall, despite Hezekiah's officials asking him to speak in Syrian/Aramaic instead (36:11-13).
Claims the LORD himself sent Assyria against Jerusalem (36:10) — presented in the text as his own boastful claim, not endorsed by the narrator.

verses.note: Sent by the king of Assyria from Lachish to Jerusalem with a great army.
Delivers a long taunting speech against Hezekiah, Judah's trust in Egypt, and the LORD's ability to deliver Jerusalem.
Hezekiah asks Isaiah to pray for 'the remnant that is left' against Rabshakeh's words, whom the king of Assyria his master has sent 'to reproach the living God.'

characters.name: Uzziah

genealogy.note: Named as Jotham's father via the chain in 7:1 ('Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah'). Isaiah gives no further genealogy for him.

funFacts: His death year (6:1) is used to date Isaiah's call vision — the only detail Isaiah gives about him beyond his name.

verses.note: Named first among the four kings of Judah under whom Isaiah prophesied.
'In the year that king Uzziah died' dates Isaiah's temple vision.
Named as Ahaz's grandfather, 'Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah.'

characters.name: Jotham

genealogy.note: Named explicitly as both Uzziah's son and Ahaz's father in the single chain of Isaiah 7:1.

funFacts: Isaiah gives him no independent action or speech at all — he appears only as a name in a genealogical chain (7:1) and in the four-king list (1:1).

verses.note: Named second among the four kings of Judah under whom Isaiah prophesied.
Identified as 'the son of Uzziah' and the father of Ahaz.

characters.name: Rezin

genealogy.note: Isaiah gives no genealogy for Rezin beyond his title 'the king of Syria.'

funFacts: Allied with Pekah of Israel against Jerusalem but 'could not prevail' (7:1).
Isaiah calls him and his ally 'two tails of smoking firebrands' — nearly spent, not truly dangerous (7:4).

verses.note: King of Syria who marches on Jerusalem with Pekah but fails to take it.
'The head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin.'
Referenced again as one of the kings the people feared, in contrast to trusting the LORD.
Named as an adversary the LORD would later set up against Israel.

characters.name: Pekah

genealogy.note: Named directly only once (7:1); every later mention calls him 'the son of Remaliah' or 'Remaliah's son' (7:4-9, 8:6) rather than by his own name.

funFacts: After his single named appearance, Isaiah consistently refers to him only by patronymic — 'the son of Remaliah' — through the rest of the Ahaz narrative.

verses.note: Named once as 'Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel,' allied with Rezin against Jerusalem.
Referred to only as 'the son of Remaliah' in Isaiah's reassurance to Ahaz.
Referred to again only as 'Remaliah's son.'

characters.name: Tirhakah

genealogy.note: Given only the title 'king of Ethiopia'; Isaiah provides no further genealogy.

funFacts: His advance against Sennacherib (37:9) prompts the Assyrian king to send Hezekiah a second, more explicit letter of intimidation rather than withdrawing.

verses.note: Report that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia has come out to fight Sennacherib, who responds by sending messengers to threaten Hezekiah further.

characters.name: Merodach-baladan

genealogy.note: Called 'the son of Baladan' in the same verse that names him (39:1) — a patronymic, not a separate figure.

funFacts: Sends letters and a present to Hezekiah on hearing of his recovery from sickness (39:1).
His embassy is the occasion for Hezekiah showing off his treasures, which prompts Isaiah's prophecy that they — and his own descendants — would one day be carried off to Babylon (39:2-7).

verses.note: King of Babylon who sends envoys to Hezekiah after his recovery.

characters.name: The Immanuel Sign
characters.purpose: A sign given to the house of David despite Ahaz's refusal to ask for one: a child to be named Immanuel ('God with us'), assuring God's continued presence with Judah even under threat of invasion. (Attribution: Isaiah, to King Ahaz)
funFacts: The name recurs twice more in the same section — 'thy land, O Immanuel' (8:8) and the LORD's own gloss 'for God is with us' (8:10) — tying the sign to the surrounding oracles.
The sign's timeline is tied to the child's growth: 'before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings' (7:16).

verses.note: 'Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.'
The child's growth used as a timeline marker for the fall of Rezin and Pekah's kingdoms.
'The stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel.'
'Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought... for God is with us.'

characters.name: Unto Us a Child Is Born (Isaiah 9:6-7)
characters.purpose: Announces a coming child/son upon whose shoulder government rests, given a string of throne-names, who will establish David's throne 'with judgment and with justice' forever — among the most quoted messianic passages in the book. (Attribution: Isaiah)
funFacts: Gives the child five throne-names in a row: 'Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace' (9:6).
Follows directly after 9:2-5's description of a people who 'walked in darkness' seeing 'a great light' and a yoke/rod of the oppressor being broken.

verses.note: 'For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given... and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.'
'Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David... with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever.'

characters.name: Oracles Against the Nations (Isaiah 13-23)
characters.purpose: A sequence of judgment oracles, most opening with the formula 'The burden of...', pronounced against Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Tyre, and others — asserting the LORD's sovereignty over every nation, not Judah alone. (Attribution: Isaiah)
funFacts: The taunt against the king of Babylon includes the line 'How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!' (14:12) — addressed to Babylon's king within the oracle, not the name of a separate figure elsewhere in the book.
Isaiah's three-year sign of walking naked and barefoot (ch. 20) is delivered specifically as a live illustration of the oracle against Egypt and Ethiopia.

verses.note: 'The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see.'
Taunt against the king of Babylon: 'How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!'
'The burden of Moab.'
'The burden of Damascus.'
'The burden of Egypt.'
'The burden of Tyre.'

characters.name: The Six Woes (Isaiah 28-33)
characters.purpose: Six prophetic denunciations, each opening with 'Woe,' pronounced across chapters 28-33 against pride, hidden rebellion, and trust in political alliances (especially Egypt) instead of the LORD. (Attribution: Isaiah)
funFacts: The woes are not evenly spaced — two fall within chapter 29 alone (29:1 and 29:15) — and the sixth (33:1) closes the whole sequence rather than opening a new oracle block.

verses.note: Woe 1: 'to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim.'
Woe 2: 'to Ariel, to Ariel, the city where David dwelt!'
Woe 3: 'unto them that seek deep to hide their counsel from the LORD.'
Woe 4: 'to the rebellious children... that take counsel, but not of me.'
Woe 5: 'to them that go down to Egypt for help... but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel.'
Woe 6: 'to thee that spoilest, and thou wast not spoiled.'

characters.name: Comfort Ye My People (Isaiah 40:1-11)
characters.purpose: Opens the book's latter section with a command to comfort Jerusalem, announces 'the voice of him that crieth in the wilderness' preparing the LORD's way, and contrasts fading human life with the LORD's enduring word. (Attribution: Isaiah)
funFacts: 'All flesh is grass' (40:6) is followed immediately by 'the word of our God shall stand for ever' (40:8) — the passage's central contrast.
Closes by picturing the LORD as a shepherd who 'shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom' (40:11).

verses.note: 'Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God... her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned.'
'The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD.'
'All flesh is grass... the word of our God shall stand for ever.'
'He shall feed his flock like a shepherd... and shall gently lead those that are with young.'

characters.name: The Servant of the LORD (Servant Songs)
characters.purpose: A recurring figure, 'my servant,' described across several passages culminating in Isaiah 52:13-53:12: one who suffers, is rejected, is silent before his accusers, and bears the guilt of others, then is exalted — the book's central suffering/atonement portrait. (Attribution: Isaiah (the LORD and the Servant both speak across the passages))
funFacts: 'He is brought as a lamb to the slaughter... so he openeth not his mouth' (53:7) gives the tier its motif.
'With his stripes we are healed' (53:5) and 'he bare the sin of many' (53:12) are among the most quoted lines in the whole book.
The servant 'made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death' despite having 'done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth' (53:9).

verses.note: 'Behold my servant, whom I uphold... he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles.'
The servant called 'from the womb,' set as 'a light to the Gentiles.'
'I gave my back to the smiters... I hid not my face from shame and spitting.'
The servant will be exalted, though his appearance was 'marred more than any man.'
'He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.'
'He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities... with his stripes we are healed.'
'He is brought as a lamb to the slaughter... so he openeth not his mouth.'
'He made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death.'
'He bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.'

characters.name: New Heavens and a New Earth
characters.purpose: A closing eschatological promise of renewed creation, in which 'the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind' (65:17) and the new order 'shall remain' permanently (66:22). (Attribution: Isaiah (the LORD speaking))
funFacts: The promise is repeated near-verbatim twice, once in ch. 65 and again in ch. 66, bracketing the material between them.

verses.note: 'For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.'
'For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me... so shall your seed and your name remain.'
